<explanation>
The Folo project is a large, multi-platform, monorepo application focused on aggregating and curating feeds into a unified, distraction‐free timeline. Its purpose is to centralize various “feeds” (news, articles, media, etc.) with advanced AI features (translation, summary) and social/community functions (sharing lists, tipping creators with $POWER). The README along with the file tree shows that Folo is built as a full-scale, multi‐frontends system with several major components:

1. Main Components:
   • Desktop Application – Built using Electron (with separate main and renderer processes, Vite configurations, and various native modules). The apps/desktop folder contains its own build scripts, resources (icons, certificates, changelogs) and comprehensive source code (including main process code and renderer UI components).
   • Mobile Application – The apps/mobile folder contains a React Native–style application (with support for iOS, Android, and even a related native folder). It provides mobile-specific assets (fonts, icons, native modules for both iOS and Android) and uses a similar architecture to manage hooks, components, and services.
   • SSR/Web Application – The apps/ssr folder contains a server-side rendered version (with a separate client folder for the React components, an API folder for Vercel integration, and server scripts). It endpoints for routing, SEO, and dynamic image generation as shown in the SSR subdirectories.
   • API Integration – The root-level “api” directory contains at least a vercel_webhook file which suggests integration points for web hooks and API services for notifications or background processes.
   • Shared & Common Packages – Under the packages directory are a set of shared modules (atoms, components, hooks, models, utilities, logger, tracker, types, etc.) that provide common functionality across all applications.

2. Architectural Relationships and Patterns:
   • Modular Monorepo Structure – The repository uses a pnpm workspace (as indicated by pnpm-workspace.yaml) and TurboRepo configuration (turbo.json) to organize code across various apps and packages. This allows each platform (desktop, mobile, ssr) to leverage shared libraries for consistency and easier maintenance.
   • Separation of UI and Business Logic – Each application has clearly separated UI layers (React components, hooks, styled components, etc.) and business logic/services (such as API fetch, authentication, database, state management) that reside in common or app-specific directories.
   • Multi-Platform Shared Resources – The shared packages, locales, constants, and utilities form the “glue” that binds various frontends. There is also an extensive i18n structure (locales/app, locales/common, etc.) that shows a commitment to internationalization.
   • Build and Deployment Pipelines – The presence of extensive CI/CD configuration files (GitHub workflows, Dependabot, and custom scripts) indicates automated build, testing, and deployment workflows for each target platform.
   • Native Integrations – For desktop and mobile platforms, there are native configuration files (such as forge.config.cts for Electron, native module configurations for iOS/Android) that show careful attention for platform-specific functionalities such as code signing and system integration.

3. Guidelines for Creating the System Design Diagram:
   a. Identify Main Blocks:
      – Desktop Client (Electron app) with its main process, renderer process, plugins and native resource integrations.
      – Mobile Client (React Native) with native modules, shared libraries, and platform-specific configurations.
      – SSR/Web Client (React-based) that handles server-side rendering, routing, and dynamic API integration.
      – API / Webhook Interface (from the api folder) to connect to external services and trigger server functions.
      – Shared/Utility Layer (packages directory) that includes components, hooks, models, constants, and utilities used by all frontends.
      – Configuration & Deployment Tools (CI/CD workflows, build scripts, tailwind configs, patches, etc.).
   b. Draw Relationships and Interactions:
      – Use directional arrows to show how each client consumes shared modules and makes API calls (for instance, desktop/mobile/SSR -> shared packages -> back-end API endpoints).
      – Illustrate communication between Electron’s main and renderer processes.
      – Show how the mobile app integrates with native modules and external stores (App Store/Microsoft/Android builds are all linked via CI scripts).
      – Highlight dependency relationships between the monorepo’s core libraries and the various platform-specific modules.
   c. Emphasize Architectural Patterns:
      – Modular and layered architecture where presentation (UI) is separated from business logic and shared utilities.
      – Microfrontend-like separation across platforms.
      – Use of configuration-as-code to manage builds (e.g., Vite and Electron configuration files, CI workflows).
   d. Mark Important Technologies & Libraries:
      – Technologies include TypeScript, React, React Native, Electron, Vite, and potentially SSR frameworks for the web application.
      – Highlight usage of state management (store directories, state hooks), internationalization (multiple locale directories), and custom build scripts.
   e. Diagram Visual Style Recommendations:
      – Use distinct shapes or colors for different types of components (e.g., rectangle for client apps, cylinder for databases or API servers, hexagon for shared packages).
      – Clearly label each component with its name and platform.
      – Use directional arrows to denote data flow (for example, showing API requests from user interfaces to the API service, and the integration of native modules).
      – Provide a legend if needed to explain color coding or shapes.

4. Tailoring the Diagram:
   – For the full-stack aspect here, emphasize a separation between multiple “frontends” (desktop, mobile, SSR) and the underlying shared code as well as integrations to backend APIs and native services.
   – Ensure that the diagram is detailed: break down each frontend into subcomponents (e.g., Electron main vs. renderer, React components, native modules) and separately list shared libraries/components that power features like i18n, state management, and UI controls.
   – Provide annotations where appropriate (for instance, noting that API communications are handled via webhooks/services in the “api” folder, or that configurations for CI/CD and code signing are built into the deployment process).

Following these guidelines, your system design diagram should neatly capture the following essential architectural elements:
   • Separate blocks for the Desktop, Mobile, and SSR clients.
   • A block for the API integration points.
   • A block representing shared libraries and common utilities used across platforms.
   • Configuration and deployment pipelines supporting multiple platforms.
   • Arrows showing inter-component communication and data flow.
   • Distinct visual cues (labels, colors, shapes) to differentiate between client-side, server-side, shared modules, and infrastructure parts.

This organized, highly detailed diagram will accurately reflect Folo’s multi-faceted design, making it easier for higher-level stakeholders and developers (like you, as the principal software engineer) to understand and work with the system’s architecture.
</explanation>
